title: Interactivity
text:
Two ways in

CSS, which styles the states an element passes through
JavaScript, which listens for the events reveal fires


we will start with the CSS way first

title: Interactivity
section: In CSS, a fragment has three states
text:
In CSS, a fragment has three states

before the click
the current fragment
after, once the next one has fired


Style each state and you have a new fragment. No JavaScript needed.


https://slidecrafting-book.com/fragments

title: Interactivity
Interactivity
Interactivity
Interactivity
section: You do not owe all three states

title: Interactivity
Interactivity
text:
What is worth changing



color
the text itself


background
the fill behind it


opacity
fade something back without removing it


border
an underline, a box, a bracket


transform
scale, rotate, nudge


filter
blur, grayscale, brightness




Every one of these animates on the compositor, so reveal can tween them for free.

title: Interactivity
text:
Careful with size and position
You can change anything, but width, height, margin, and font-size move the rest of the slide with them. That reflow reads as jitter.

transform: scale() grows a thing without touching its neighbours. Reach for that instead.


Color, background, and opacity are the safe playground.

title: Interactivity
text:
That was all CSS
Reveal marked the element with a class, and your stylesheet reacted. Nothing ran, and going backwards undid itself.

Three states, because they are three selectors
Whatever CSS cannot express is out of reach


JavaScript has no states. It has two events, and undoing the change is your job.

title: Interactivity
section: Reveal tells you when a fragment fires

title: Interactivity
text:
Always write both directions

Presenters go backwards, in the middle of a talk, in front of people
fragmenthidden should be the exact inverse of fragmentshown
Scrolled down? Scroll back up. Switched a tab? Switch it back


If a change cannot be undone, it makes a bad fragment.

title: Interactivity
text:
Wire it up

my-deck.qmd
format:
  revealjs:
    include-after-body:
      - "_fragments.html"


And _fragments.html is a <script> tag with your Reveal.on() calls inside.

title: Interactivity
text:
An empty fragment still fires
A fragment does not have to contain what it changes.

my-deck.qmd
::: {.fragment .color data-color="orange"}
:::


event.fragment.dataset.color reads that value, so one class covers many slides.

title: Interactivity
section: Matching elements across a slide break
text:
Matching elements across a slide break
Mark two adjacent slides with auto-animate=true and reveal tweens the difference.

Position, size, color, corner radius, font size
Matching is automatic, but fragile
Give the pair the same data-id and it is not


https://slidecrafting-book.com/auto-animate

title: Interactivity
Interactivity
text: More advanced example

title: Interactivity
text:
The pixel counting is over
This used to be the reason nobody did it: every panel is four numbers, and you found them by rendering, squinting, and editing again.
With AI agents this work is a little easier.

Describe the layout, let the model write the data-id divs and their coordinates
Paste the slide back and ask for the next state of it
You still judge whether the motion reads well

title: Interactivity
text:
Exercise

Turn a list on one of your slides into an .incremental list
Add .highlight-last and the SCSS for it, so the current bullet stands out
Take one slide, copy it, mark both auto-animate=true, and change one thing
Give the element you changed a data-id and watch the animation get steadier

title: Extensions & wrap-up
text:
Someone else already solved it

An extension is a folder of Lua, JavaScript, and CSS that Quarto knows how to load
It ships as a GitHub repo, and you install it by name
Nothing to configure globally, it lives inside your project


Every styled code block you have seen today came from one.

title: Extensions & wrap-up
text:
Installing

Terminal
quarto add emilhvitfeldt/quarto-revealjs-codewindow


Downloads into _extensions/ next to your .qmd
Commit that folder, it is part of the project

title: Content & layout
text:
The six attributes



Attribute
Description




width
width of the element


height
height of the element


top
distance from the top of the slide


left
distance from the left of the slide


bottom
distance from the bottom of the slide


right
distance from the right of the slide



One of top / bottom, one of left / right, and only one of width / height so the image is not distorted.

title: Content & layout
section: Plots are figures with extra knobs
text:
Plots are figures with extra knobs

fig-width / fig-height how big the plot is drawn, which sets how big its text is
fig-asp the ratio, so you only tune one of the two
fig-dpi raise it when the plot looks soft
fig-align left, center, or right


The defaults sit around fig-width: 9, fig-height: 5, which makes axis labels too small from the back row.


https://slidecrafting-book.com/elements

title: Content & layout
text:
Smaller plot, bigger text


my-deck.qmd

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-asp: 0.5
plot(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars, col = factor(am), pch = 16, bty = "n")
```







Drawing the plot smaller makes its text bigger, because reveal scales it back up to fit.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Reproducible
We get all the goodness from quarto,
Code cells run at render time:

my-deck.qmd
```{r}
#| echo: false
plot(1:10)
```

Figures and tables regenerate from the data instead of being pasted screenshots, HUGE when new data comes in.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
HTML-native
A rendered deck is a web page.
Animation, video, iframes, links, and anything else the web can do.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
And when someone insists
The same source renders to PDF or PowerPoint.
Except for html specific things like animation and interactivity.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
A minimal deck


my-deck.qmd
---
title: "My first deck"
author: "Your Name"
format: revealjs
---

## First slide

Some content, with a **bold** word.

- one bullet
- another bullet

## Second slide

```{r}
#| echo: true
summary(cars$speed)
```

Options worth knowing on day one

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Divs and spans
Markdown alone cannot say “make this part special”. Quarto adds two ways to wrap content and attach attributes to it.

a div wraps one or more blocks: paragraphs, lists, images, code
a span wraps a piece of text inside a paragraph


Almost every feature in this workshop is one of these two with a different class on it.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
The syntax


Div

my-deck.qmd
::: {.center}
Everything here
is inside the div.
:::

Opening fence, attributes, content, closing fence.

Span

my-deck.qmd
The [important part]{.highlight}
of the sentence.

Text in [], attributes in {}, no space between them.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
What goes in the braces

my-deck.qmd
::: {#summary .smaller .fragment style="color: red;"}
Content.
:::


.name a class, the usual way to reach a div from CSS
#name an id, unique on the page
key="value" any other attribute, style= included


Order does not matter, and you can use as many as you like.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Nesting: count your colons



Works
:::: {.outer}

::: {.inner}
Content.
:::

::::



Breaks
::: {.outer}

::: {.inner}
Content.
:::

:::



The outer fence needs more colons than the inner one, otherwise Pandoc closes the wrong div. Three is only the minimum.

title: What is Quarto?
text:
Divs and spans in action


my-deck.qmd
## Highlights

Some [red text]{style="color: #b22222;"} in a sentence.

::: {.smaller}
This whole block is smaller.
:::

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
And this one is centered.
:::

text:

Columns are just nested divs: a .columns div holding .column divs.

Left side.

title: Theming

The 10 Minute Theme
You can get very far with theming using only

fonts
colors
sizes


https://slidecrafting-book.com/10-minute

title: Theming
text:
Themes are written with CSS

Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) is a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of a document written in HTML

CSS is written as a series of pairs; selectors and properties.

selectors specify what elements on a page we want to style.
properties specify what the elements should look like.

title: Theming
Theming
section: Why so many words on the left?

title: Theming
section: A language that compiles to CSS
text:
A language that compiles to CSS
While CSS is very powerful, it can also feel a little too wordy and less expressive. So we use the compiled langauge Sass.

You write Sass
A compiler turns it into plain CSS
The browser gets the CSS


Quarto runs that compiler for you on every render. There is no build step to set up.

title: Theming
Theming
text:
So, names

Sass the language and the compiler
SCSS the syntax you write it in, and the file extension
CSS what comes out the other end


Quarto expects .scss. That is the only one you need to think about.

title: Theming
Theming
section: The compiler writes the boring parts

title: Theming
Theming
text:
Mistakes get caught
A typo in CSS is silent. The browser drops the line and moves on.

$primry-color fails to compile and tells you the line
Undefined mixins and functions do the same
You find out at render time, not from the back row

title: Theming
text:
The theme outlives the talk
You are not styling one deck. You are building a look you keep.

Next talk starts by copying one file
Fix something once and every future deck has it fixed
Variables at the top are the knobs you actually turn


That is the whole bet: pay the setup cost once, spend the rest of your time on content.

title: Theming
section: One line of YAML, one file
text:
One line of YAML, one file


my-deck.qmd
format:
  revealjs:
    theme: [default, styles.scss]

Combine a built-in theme with your sheet, or skip the built-in with theme: styles.scss.

https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/themes.html

title: Theming
text:
The two layers

styles.scss
/*-- scss:defaults --*/

/*-- scss:rules --*/


defaults sass variables, read before Quarto builds the theme
rules plain CSS, applied after


Reach for a variable first. Write a rule only when no variable exists.

title: Theming
text:
Three variables

$presentation-heading-font slide titles
$font-family-sans-serif body text
$font-family-monospace inline code and code blocks

title: Theming
Theming
text:
quarto revealjs sass variables
you can go really far with the revealjs sass variables
however it doesn’t cover everything possible that we could want to do
so we will need to write our own SCSS rules

https://quarto.org/docs/presentations/revealjs/themes.html#sass-variables

title: Theming
section: Demo: which class do I hit?
text:
Demo: which class do I hit?

If you can see it on a slide, it has a selector. The browser will tell you what it is.


Right-click the thing you want to style, pick “Inspect”
Read the HTML pane: the element and the classes it carries
Read the styles pane: the rules already hitting it, most specific first
Edit a value right there to check you picked the right one
Then write that selector into styles.scss


Nothing you change in the inspector is saved. It is a scratchpad, not an editor.

title: Theming
Theming
Theming
text:
Slide variants
Same deck, a handful of slide looks. Give a slide a class and style that class.

my-deck.qmd
## A normal slide

## A section break {.variant-one}

## An exercise {.variant-two}


The plain slide is your base style. A class is what you reach for when you want a different one.


https://slidecrafting-book.com/theme

title: Theming
Theming
text:
What variants are good for

Section breaks, so the deck visibly changes gear
Functional slides: exercises, demos, results
Marking the parts of an argument: problem, solution


The classic is xaringan’s inverse: one dark slide among the white ones, used for a section break or a quote.


https://slidecrafting-book.com/theme
